leads.summary: New removal assertion does not detect a missing Edge cleanup, and the shared install assertion misses an Edge-only wiring regression

Likewise changing only the Edge installer branch from setup_chromium_policy_directory to browser_policy_setup_dir leaves the shared helper's grep intact. The new jq assertion also checks only six of ten shipped keys, so deleting any single PrivacySandbox* policy leaves it green. The suite's real installer fixture covers Chromium but not Edge. leads.summary: Document the privileged, later-sorting and root-owned requirements of the suggested override
leads.consequence: Ordinary users cannot 'drop' a file into the 0755 root-owned directory. To survive later browser installations, a managed JSON override needs root ownership (the shared directory setup deletes non-root children) and a filename that sorts after privacy.json for conflicting keys. Calling a JSON 'higher-priority' without explaining these constraints makes the only advertised override nonfunctional or short-lived for users following it literally. Chromium's loader processes files in reverse lexical order with later filenames winning.
leads.triage: already_in_opus; override requirements, part of N1

comment:
## Automated AI review

> **Community review:** Independent automated community review, unaffiliated with the Omarchy team, intended to help prepare PRs for their review.

Follow-up to the [earlier review](https://github.com/omacom/omarchy/pull/13110#issuecomment-5825241936) and the [author's reply](https://github.com/omacom/omarchy/pull/13110#issuecomment-5825346641), checked at `78eabf03`.

**Verified:** the migration, test and manual changes do what the reply describes. No regression was found, and the earlier Verified results still hold at this head. One new point: the added manual paragraph claims a Privacy Sandbox effect the policy does not have, and does not say what an override needs.

| Earlier point | Status at `78eabf03` |
|---|---|
| Migration runs `sudo` for its existence check | Resolved |
| Wiring reversions pass the suite | Resolved (full reversions now fail) |
| Manual does not mention the policy | Resolved, but see the new finding below |
| Edge applies only four of the ten keys | Resolved by documentation: the manual now says Edge honours only the shared subset (incomplete, see below) |
| Every setting is locked (`managed/` rather than `recommended/`) | Still present, left to the maintainers (see below) |
| `PrivacySandbox*` keys have no identified effect | Still present, and now repeated in the manual |

**Verified (migration):** in isolated runs with a logging `sudo` stub and `/etc` redirected to a private directory, the new `[[ -f ]]` check behaves as follows (old `as_root test -f` form in brackets):

```text
all managed dirs absent          -> 0 sudo calls   (old: 4)
privacy.json already installed   -> 0 sudo calls   (old: 4)
four dirs present, no file       -> 4 sudo calls   (old: 8), all installed
account without sudo, file there -> exits 0        (old: fails, stays pending)
account without sudo, no file    -> exits 1, stays pending (same as old)
```

**Verified (tests):** `test/shell.d/browser-policy-dir-test.sh` passes at this head. Removing the privacy call from the fresh-install hook or from `omarchy install browser`, emptying the migration, or reverting both remove-browser lines now fails the suite.

### The new manual paragraph misstates the Privacy Sandbox effect and leaves out what an override needs

`manual/23-browsers.md` now says the policy turns off "Privacy Sandbox ad APIs" and that users can "override any of it by dropping a higher-priority JSON into the browser's managed policy directory".

- **Privacy Sandbox:** in Chromium 153 all four `PrivacySandbox*` keys are deprecated. The handler only writes `false` into prefs that already default to `false`, and Chromium clears user-set values of those prefs at startup (`kPrivacySandboxAdPrivacyUxDeprecation`, enabled by default). The Edge sentence also excludes only WebRTC and spell check, although Microsoft's Edge policy documentation has none of the four `PrivacySandbox*` keys either.
- **Override:** "higher-priority" has a specific meaning here. Chromium keeps the value from the file whose name sorts last in byte order, so the override file name must sort after `privacy.json`:

  ```text
  wins over privacy.json:   zz-local.json   user.json      privacy_local.json
  loses to privacy.json:    override.json   local.json     custom.json
                            00-override.json   privacy-local.json
  ```

  The directory is 0755 root:root, so writing the file needs `sudo`. It must stay root-owned to survive the policy-directory purge, which removes files not owned by root. An override sets a different value that is still enforced: per Chromium's policy descriptions, users can't change a policy-set value in the browser. For Brave, `omarchy remove browser brave` deletes `/etc/brave`, override included, when Brave Origin is not also installed.
- `AlternateErrorPagesEnabled` is not mentioned, although it is one of the changed settings and one that Edge honours.

**Impact:** users following the manual literally are likely to pick a file name that loses to `privacy.json`, and are told Privacy Sandbox is turned off when the keys have no identified effect.

**Suggested change:** drop the Privacy Sandbox wording (or the four keys, as suggested earlier), and spell out the override: a root-owned JSON whose name sorts after `privacy.json`, for example `/etc/chromium/policies/managed/zz-local.json`, written with `sudo`. The Edge sentence could list what Edge honours, including `AlternateErrorPagesEnabled`.

### Locked settings (author question)

The reply offers to switch keys to `policies/recommended` if the maintainers prefer. Nothing in this revision changes the earlier analysis: the policy is still mandatory, and `SearchSuggestEnabled`, `NetworkPredictionOptions`, `BlockThirdPartyCookies` and `SpellCheckServiceEnabled` are the four keys Chromium 153 allows in `recommended/`. The choice between locked and user-adjustable defaults is a design decision for the maintainers.

**Optional test improvement:** these single-line edits still pass the suite in isolated mutation runs:

```text
privacy call moved before browser_policy_setup_dir  -> suite passes (a fresh install gets no privacy.json)
only the chrome or only the edge remove line reverted -> suite passes
migration condition changed so the loop never installs -> suite passes
```

Checking both remove-browser paths separately and checking that the privacy call follows the directory setup would catch the first two.

**Related open PR:** #10446 moves the fresh-install policy setup to `/etc/brave/policies/managed`. If both merge as written, the Chromium privacy call in `install/config/browser-policy.sh` would skip silently on fresh installs, and the new grep assertion would still pass. The two PRs were not tested together.

---

## Review information

**Test scope:** follow-up of the commit since `96cc0bba`. The test file (also against mutated copies of the privacy wiring), the fresh-install hook, the helper, `omarchy remove browser` and 15 migration states (old and new form) were run in an isolated sandbox with privileged commands stubbed and `/etc` paths redirected to a private directory. Root ownership comes from source, not execution. Policy semantics and file ordering come from Chromium 153 source, the Brave path from brave-core 1.96.59 source, and Edge support from Microsoft's policy documentation (which lists Windows and macOS, not Linux). No browser was launched, and the override file ordering was not observed in `chrome://policy`.

**AI process:** Opus 5.5 Medium coordination and synthesis, Opus 5.5 Xhigh technical review and final fact check, GPT 6 Sol Xhigh search for related issues, Opus 5.5 Medium editorial check.
